chapter: Teschemacher, Pee Wee, Noon and Simeon
title: Teschemacher and Pee Wee as founders of Chicago clarinet style
summary: They agree Teschemacher and Pee Wee Russell underlie Chicago clarinet, with Rod Cless and Bud Jacobson as representatives.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: Both you and I, I believe, feel that the Chicago School, as far as clarinet was concerned, was based on the inventions or the conceptions or the styles of the school. The styles of Teschmacher and Pee-wee-Pee-wee, not distinctly a Chicagoan, historically speaking, but yet so compatible with the Chicago style. Well, first of all, is that assumption correct, that they might have founded the elements of the Chicago style, as far as clarinet?

It's my assumption, yes. The actual historical business is vague to me. I don't know exactly when or how often Pee-wee played in Chicago, but you can't discuss Chicago style without discussing Pee-wee's playing, I don't think.
Do you remember any others of their general category? The early first generation horn men?
Well, Rod Klass used to bum around with Tesch, and Bud Jacobson was in town, wasn't he? Bud is, to me, representative of Chicago style, beautifully.
And yet he, I think, would be one of the first to say that, well, he was trying to play the rules that Teschmacher laid down. He'd constantly refer to Teschmacher's solo as the right way to play it.
This is Klass or... Or Jacobson. Jacobson, really?
